title: Bagged Tree Tuning Causes an Error
description: In the attached HTML file, I was tasked with comparing different types of models on a dataset using tidymodels. The Code Chunk just below the heading "Fit the BTREE Model to CV Folds" causes an Error shown in the attached png file. The workaround required two modifications to the code: 1. Simplify the column names on the data set. 2. Change the arguments on the Code Chunk just below the heading "Define Bagged Tree (BTREE) Model and Engine" from: tree_depth = integer(5), min_n = integer(10) to tree_depth = 5 min_n = 10 [HW9_Modeling_Practice.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/23681465/HW9_Modeling_Practice.html) It appears the tidymodels code for Bagged Trees is not robust to column names and the arguments for tree_depth and min_n. I spent a lot of time to get to the workaround so I thought it should be reported.

title: Add a section about letting your reviewer know that you used AI to write the PR
description:
Maybe link to some PRs from Lionel and Hadley that do this, and mention the use of ✨ 

There's a mindshift that you as a reviewer go through when you know that the PR was mostly AI written. I think you get...more strict? Especially if the PR comes from someone who otherwise writes nearly perfect PRs without AI.

It's also nice to not have to _guess_ whether the PR was AI written or not, which tends to cause me a nonzero amount of stress

title: Content suggestion: large PRs breaking down
description:
Show instructions on how to send a commit separately.

If already a large PR, some commits can be moved to another branch and open a new PR for those?

Do you think it would be a good idea to include?

Edit: I used `gert::git_cherry_pick()` but that's an incomplete solutiom.


```shell
git checkout <Main branch>
git checkout -b <new branch>
git checkout origin/<branch with too many commit> -- <file to separate from PR.R>
git commit -m '<new commit message>'
git push origin <new branch>
```

https://github.com/Rdatatable/data.table/issues/4370#issuecomment-1953175481_
            
For splitting https://github.com/r-lib/tidyselect/pull/358. I made extensive use of the Git Pane in RStudio.

From my initial branch cleanup, I created a new branch (disable remote tracking) than I ran `gert::git_reset_mixed()` and used the Git pane to revert some changes. Then, I used `usethis::pr_push()`.

Go back to the cleanup branch and repeat twice.

title: Talk about using Copilot as a way to give yourself an AI assisted self-review before asking for a human review
description:
This is a particularly nice way to decrease the burden on your reviewers, because Copilot reviews can often catch small issues, or at least force you to confirm your own beliefs, before you hand off your PR to a human reviewer

(There's something nice about this use of AI vs letting AI write the code for you. This unconditionally reduces the burden on your reviewer. Letting AI write code for you can increase the burden on your reviewer, because they no longer can be completely sure if this is code from you or from AI)

Make sure to add some pictures about the process.

Also talk about how to do it locally in VS Code before you even submit the PR (though I find this to be more limited because it only applies to the uncommitted changes sitting in your workspace)

title: Provide some guidance on how to stack PRs
description:
Sometimes you want to send in a new feature where you _know_ it is going to be too large for 1 PR, but you can't completely separate the ideas into their own ideas that branch directly off `main` like this:

```mermaid
graph TD
m[main]
m --> a[Branch A]
m --> b[Branch B]
```

In this case you probably want to send in some _stacked PRs_.

```mermaid
graph TD
m[main]
m --> a[Branch A]
a --> b[Branch B]
```

This is a more advanced technique, but it allows you to separate your large feature into meaningful sub sections that are much easier to review and have a focused conversation about. And importantly it allows you to use features from `Branch A` in `Branch B` without having to wait for `Branch A` to land on main.

We should provide some descriptions of this and how to do it in practice (in painstaking detail, because this is complicated!)

title: Add more rules about when to finish off a PR vs giving more feedback
description:
This section:
https://code-review.tidyverse.org/reviewer/comments.html#sec-finishing-off-an-external-contribution

already has some good points about when to finish off an external contribution. In particular:
- If the package has been dormant for a long time and you are reviving it and finishing off some long standing PRs
- If you have gone through 1-2 rounds of review already

But it feels like we could say a few more things related to how much you nit pick with comments vs just doing it yourself.

It seems like we can expand on a section related to _relationship building_ between the reviewer and the author.

- If this is a person that could be a longer term contributor, then you generally will spend more time working with them and giving more feedback and nit picking more to ensure they understand what you are looking for in reviews. This increases the chance that their future reviews will need less feedback, because they will be more familiar with what you want.
- If this is a "drive by" PR, then feel free to do the heavy lifting yourself, especially if it looks like the PR is in a state where review is going to take a couple rounds (i.e. lots of effort on the reviewer's end), but won't result in a longer term contributor. Typical rules about being appreciative for the contribution still apply though.

title: Another example of a "good" PR
description:
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/pull/1791

- Mentioned the dplyr PR it was related to, even though it doesnt close it
- Was up front about what was expected of the reviewer, which is different from normal because most of the time the reviewer does a deep review. In this case I knew my reviewer wasn't as familiar with that section of the codebase, so a high level review was ok
- Details the main feature of the PR and links out to external resources that back it up
- Outlines exactly how it replaces an old feature it is replacing
- Provides an example of a potentially tricky case to make the reviewer aware of
- Inline comments to point out some major details worth looking at. Especially important since the reviewer isn't as familiar with this part of the code base, and because the PR is large
- Pointed out a bug to tackle in another PR, but notably did _not_ tackle it in this PR https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/pull/1791#discussion_r1113674398
- Some back and forth about naming, with deferral to the reviewer https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/pull/1791#discussion_r1114087922

title: Book club notes
description:
1 Good CL descriptions
- In the intro, future you is likely to read it. 
- Body is informative
  - Use reprex to show before / after (either broken vs not broken or slow vs fast) 
  - Use `Closes` github keywords and whatnot
  - Essentially link to any tabs that you have open that were helpful in solving this PR

2 Small CLs
- highlight speed and throughness as good reasons for keeping them small
- when does it have to be large? embracing cli for the whole user interface of the package. using rlang `error_call`. some big policy change. testthat 3. there is a single organizing theme - "it still does one thing"

3 Reviewer comments
- Probably won't mention "dont take it personally" up front.
- 3.2 probably is better as the first section
- Review your own code first
- As the author, leave comments on Github about particularly difficult sections of the code
- A number of examples about when something belongs in the code review tooling vs when it should be moved into the code itself
  - Ask people for good examples of this through issues. 

Dealing with resolving comments:
- Who resolves the comments? 99% of the time it is the author who says they are doing it or they don't. Generally leave a comment saying `Done` or a thumbs up before resolving.
- If you _aren't_ going to accept their suggestion, leave a comment about why and then it is up to you as to whether or not you resolve the comment (depending on if you want the original Reviewer to see your counterpoint or not)

4 The standards of code review
- This might could be pulled up to the very beginning as a "why do we do this at all"
- Mentoring is a very important part of the process
- Does the PR maintain or increase the similarity of the code base to the rest of our ecosystem? This makes it easier for users, for us to switch between packages, and for others to contribute.
  - Back to mentoring because you have to teach someone this is how we do things here.
  - PRs that simply increase cohesion across packages are valuable in themselves (spring cleaning)
  - Resolving conflicts - talk about whether the problem is between two people with equal stakes or if it is between the package maintainer and an outside contributor

5 what to look for
- You often pick up on more things if you `pr_fetch()` and try it out locally yourself
- Do we encourage `Nit:`? It doesn't seem that bad.
- Take out everything about parallel programming
- 5.9 documentation could also affect vignettes or documentation of other functions
- 5.4 tests
  - call out tidymodels extratests as a special case to think about
  - make sure that the test machinery looks similar to the other ones around it
  - is the test fairly minimal
- 5.10.1 Exceptions about every line - you can use your discretion about reviewing things like tests as closely if the author is trustworthy

10 Emergencies
- The only hard deadline we have is really a CRAN 2 week ultimatum
- Otherwise lets remove this section

---

- As a reviewer, call out when you see sections of the code you don't understand
- If you are the author and you have done a revdepcheck, say so and say what the fallout was
- Mention `style.tidyverse.org` and styler
